question: In July, the Commission published the EU’s strategy for the livestock sector. The strategy contains many good initiatives to improve the difficult situation in the livestock sector at farm level, as well as measures to improve the food chain. As stated in the strategy, meat produced in Europe responsibly and to high production standards is a key component of European competitiveness and the vitality of rural areas.

The strategy emphasises how important local and regional chains and consumer expectations for production are. It also highlights the fact that European production creates value in the chain through good practices, quality, sustainability and responsibility, rather than competing on the basis of the lowest possible price.

It is good that the role of origin labelling is also highlighted as a key measure in the strategy. The importance of origin labelling and the Buy European Food campaign was also outlined by President von der Leyen in her State of the European Union address in Strasbourg in September 2025.

Every European has the right to eat meat produced in Europe and the right to a transparent production chain that makes it easy to trace the origin of food. A transparent and traceable food chain also prevents and helps combat food fraud. With the above in mind: 1.

What specific steps does the Commission intend to take to make origin labelling for meat and meat products clearer and more transparent for consumers than it is at present, including country-of-origin labelling?
Does the Commission intend to extend the requirement for origin and country labelling to processed meat products where meat is the main ingredient?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) In the Vision for Agriculture and Food1, published in February 2025, the Commission announced its intention to extend country-of-origin labelling, taking into account sectorspecific characteristics and the rules of the Single Market.
The Livestock Strategy2, published in July 2026, also recognises that greater transparency across the food chain, including clearer information and labelling, is essential.

This commitment is reflected in the post-2027 multiannual financial framework package, notably in the proposal to amend Regulation (EU) No 1308/20133 establishing the common organisation of the markets (CMO Regulation), presented in July 2025 and currently under negotiation by the European Parliament and the Council.

The proposal clarifies that marketing standards may include requirements relating to the ‘place of farming and/or origin’ and extends the scope for such standards to additional sectors, including protein crops, beef, pigmeat, sheepmeat and goatmeat.

This would provide the Commission with an appropriate legal basis to develop, where justified, proportionate and supported by consumer interest, sector-specific EU rules on origin labelling. In addition, the co-legislators have already advanced this objective through the recent amendment of the CMO Regulation4, which introduces such a possibility for poultrymeat.

The Livestock Strategy also proposes to enable, through optional reserved terms in the CMO Regulation, an identifiable ‘European excellence’ term on a voluntary basis. This would be supported by clear specifications to valorise the excellence of the EU’s production of animal products. 2.
As the envisaged legal basis is Article 75 of the CMO Regulation, any future Commission measure under that framework could only concern products falling within that Article’s scope.

1 https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/vision-agriculture-and-food_en. 2 https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/vision-overview/eu-livestock-strategy_en. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/1308/oj/eng. 4 Regulation (EU) 2026/1739 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending
Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013, (EU) 2021/2115 and (EU) 2021/2116 as regards the strengthening of the position of farmers in the food supply chain.
